# Hepatorenal syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Hepatorenal syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/CG0qY3)

---

## Summary

Hepatorenal syndrome (<u>HRS</u>) refers to a unique type of <u>kidney injury</u> that occurs in patients with <u>cirrhosis</u> and <u>ascites</u>. The pathophysiology is not well understood but is likely due to <u>splanchnic</u> <u>vasodilation</u> in the setting of <u>portal hypertension</u>. <u>HRS</u> may develop rapidly in the case of <u>HRS acute kidney injury</u> (<u>HRS-AKI</u>) or gradually in the case of <u>HRS</u> non-<u>acute kidney injury</u> (<u>HRS-NAKI</u>). It is a diagnosis of exclusion and requires the elimination of other potential etiologies, including <u>hypovolemia</u>. A <u>liver transplant</u> is the only curative treatment, but it may be mitigated pharmacologically with vasoconstrictors and <u>albumin</u>.

---

## Definitions

* A unique <u>phenotype</u> of <u>kidney injury</u> in patients with <u>cirrhosis</u> and <u>ascites</u> in the absence of <u>hypovolemia</u> or other <u>kidney</u> pathology. It is further split into: [[2]](/library/WCcPIe0)[[3]](/library/YIbnYE)

* HRS-acute kidney injury (<u>HRS-AKI</u>): <u>acute kidney injury</u> in patients with <u>cirrhosis</u> (see “<u>Diagnostic criteria for HRS-AKI</u>” below); formerly known as <u>type 1 HRS</u>

* HRS-non-acute kidney injury (<u>HRS-NAKI</u>): functional <u>kidney injury</u> in patients with <u>cirrhosis</u> not meeting the criteria for <u>HRS-AKI</u>; formerly known as <u>type 2 HRS</u>

---

## Etiology

* Complication of <u>liver</u> failure, especially <u>cirrhosis</u>

* The exact pathomechanisms are not completely understood: <u>Cirrhosis</u>/<u>portal hypertension</u> → ↑ <u>splanchnic</u> <u>vasodilators</u> (e.g., <u>nitric oxide</u>) → ↓ arterial blood flow → activation of <u>RAAS</u> → renal <u>vasoconstriction</u> → ↓ <u>GFR</u> [[3]](/library/YIbnYE)

* <u>Risk factors</u>/triggers may include:

* Drainage of large volume <u>ascites</u> (without concurrent <u>albumin</u> administration) [[4]](/library/hvcc-V0)

* <u>Gastrointestinal bleeding</u>

* <u>Forced diuresis</u>

* Excess use of <u>laxatives</u> (<u>lactulose</u>)

* Infections, e.g., <u>spontaneous bacterial peritonitis</u>

---

## Clinical features

* Ranging from <u>oliguria</u> up to <u>anuria</u> with progressive <u>kidney failure</u>

* See also “<u>Cirrhosis</u>” and “<u>Decompensated cirrhosis</u>.”

* <u>Hypotension</u> and wide <u>pulse pressure</u>

---

## Diagnosis

Hepatorenal syndrome (<u>HRS</u>) is a diagnosis of exclusion. It is diagnosed based on the presence of renal impairment in patients with <u>cirrhosis</u> after other potential causes of renal impairment have been ruled out. [[2]](/library/WCcPIe0)[[4]](/library/hvcc-V0)




* Initial evaluation

* Clinical evaluation: Rule out <u>shock</u>, <u>hypovolemia</u>, and <u>nephrotoxic agent</u> intake.

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>Creatinine</u>

* Urine studies: <u>urinalysis</u>, <u>urine sediment</u>, <u>fractional excretion of sodium</u> or <u>urea</u>  [[4]](/library/hvcc-V0)[[5]](/library/nrb73E)

* Imaging: Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> to assess for obstruction

* Diagnostic criteria for HRS-AKI   [[2]](/library/WCcPIe0)[[5]](/library/nrb73E)[[6]](/library/2SXT_x)

* Presence of <u>cirrhosis</u> with <u>ascites</u>

* <u>Diagnosis of AKI</u> according to the following criteria: [[5]](/library/nrb73E)

* An increase in serum <u>creatinine</u> of ≥ 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or to ≥ 1.5 times baseline within a 7-day period

* And/or urine output ≤ 0.5 mL/kg for ≥ 6 hours

* No improvement after two consecutive days of <u>albumin</u> infusions and <u>diuretic</u> withdrawal

* Absence of <u>shock</u>

* No current or recent <u>nephrotoxic agents</u>

* Absence of signs of structural <u>kidney</u> disease

---

## Treatment

Treatment for <u>HRS-AKI</u> should always be combined with adequate management for <u>cirrhosis</u>, and a multidisciplinary team should be involved as soon as possible. Data on effective treatments for <u>HRS-NAKI</u> is lacking. [[2]](/library/WCcPIe0)




### Pharmacotherapy for <u>HRS-AKI</u> [[2]](/library/WCcPIe0)




* Preferred: vasoconstrictor (either <u>terlipressin</u> OR <u>norepinephrine</u>) PLUS <u>albumin</u>

* Alternative: combination of <u>midodrine</u>;  PLUS <u>octreotide</u>





### Surgical or interventional options [[2]](/library/WCcPIe0)




* <u>Renal replacement therapy</u> (mainly <u>hemodialysis</u>)  [[2]](/library/WCcPIe0)

* A <u>liver transplant</u> is the only curative option.

* <u>TIPS</u> placement is not routinely recommended.   [[2]](/library/WCcPIe0)[[4]](/library/hvcc-V0)





### Prevention




* General measures: prevention of <u>GI bleeding</u> and bacterial infections, avoidance of <u>large-volume paracentesis</u> without concurrent <u>albumin</u> administration

* Specific measures: IV <u>albumin</u> with <u>antibiotics</u> reduces the risk of patients with <u>spontaneous bacterial peritonitis</u> developing <u>HRS-AKI</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Rule out other causes of <u>AKI</u> and ensure the <u>diagnostic criteria for HRS-AKI</u> are fulfilled before initiating vasoconstrictor therapy.




> [!WARNING]
> Vasoconstrictor therapy is challenging and has potentially severe adverse effects (e.g., <u>ischemia</u>); involve specialists early.




> [!WARNING]
> Patients with <u>cirrhosis</u> and <u>HRS</u> can develop significant fluid retention and <u>pulmonary edema</u>. Therefore, administer <u>IV fluids</u> with caution. [[3]](/library/YIbnYE)
